entries.title: Literary Mystery Novels, recommended by Nicholas Russell
entries.summary: Suspense is a powerful narrative engine that drives the plots of many novels, whether or not they are shelved under 'mystery books' in a shop. We asked Nicholas Russell – longtime bookseller and debut novelist – to recommend five of the best literary mystery novels, all notable for the quality of the writing and the creativity of approach. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
Suspense is a powerful narrative engine that drives the plots of many novels, whether or not they are shelved under 'mystery books' in a shop. We asked Nicholas Russell – longtime bookseller and debut novelist – to recommend five of the best literary mystery novels, all notable for the quality of the writing and the creativity of approach.

Thank you for agreeing to recommend five literary mystery novels. As with romance books, I think there are novels that fall within the commercial ‘mystery’ genre but also a much wider ecosystem of books that use mystery as a device to drive a plot forward.

Yes, it’s interesting. Applying the ‘literary’ tag to genre – whether that is mystery, horror, whatever – adds a slight layer of condescension. Like: these are mystery novels for adults.

As opposed to all the other mystery novels, which must then be, by implication, childish.

Right. But I think it can go one of two ways. It can either mean there is a greater attention to the prose – that the prose is considered of equal importance to the plot – or that it is a very light-handed version of the genre. So, it might be a literary novel but with mystery elements.

As a bookseller, I know that readers have certain expectations when they go to a certain section of the bookstore. The function of genre is one of expectation. At least in part.

So when you say ‘literary [blank]’, there’s a sense that it will be more intellectual, or there will be less emphasis on the page-turning quality of your standard genre novel.

That being said, the books I’ve picked are all over the place. Some are literary because they have great prose, or approach the mystery from an interesting angle. But I do think they are very much of the genre and do not shy away from it.

Your own recent novel, Observer, makes an interesting genre Venn diagram. There are mystery elements, horror elements, and it is literary in style or in terms of writing quality. Do you think of it this way?

The only thing I was adamant about when we were selling the novel was that I wanted it shelved in the horror section. That it should be very much a horror novel, but within that it could contain any number of things.

I do consider myself more of a short story writer, and I read widely. I think my fiction tends towards the literary-speculative. It’s only since the book came out that people told me it is also, in part, a mystery novel. That came organically from the plot, which is about a young woman looking for her mother and finding out all these things that have been kept secret.

I didn’t want to shy away from the genre elements, it mattered a lot to me that it shouldn’t be shelved in ‘general fiction’.

Can we look at your book recommendations? Let’s start with Tana French’s In the Woods, which was her debut novel back in 2007.

It’s an incredible book. A friend of mine, who is not at all a genre person, could not stop talking about it. I found that interesting. I immediately thought: There must be something going on here beyond the plot to make it interesting to him.

Tana French’s novels are remarkable. First, the prose is really great – she cares about her sentences and the way things sound. But also, the mystery genre is a very fruitful genre for psychology and exploring the inner lives of characters – and she has a really great unreliable narrator in In the Woods. There’s a sense that the narrator is lying to themselves about something, and that’s essential to their job, which is that they are a detective. The lying plays out in a very interesting way at the end of the novel.

Tana French also writes my favourite kind of series, which is one that you don’t need to read in order. There are recurring characters, but it might be that a character is much older in the next book, or is in the background of another. Something like that.

Yes, I really love that about the writing of Emily St. John Mandel – fans talk about the ‘Mandelverse’ – or even Jennifer Egan’s A Visit from the Goon Squad and The Candy House. The stories don’t link, exactly, but you have this sense that the recurring characters continue to exist and have lives outside of the books themselves.

Exactly. It’s a very generous way of crafting a series, which is to say: Come at it at any point that you want. You don’t need to start here. Although I do think you should start with In the Woods.

It’s a very spooky book too. That’s another reason why I really like it – there’s a feeling that it could, at any moment, turn into an outright horror novel. She has a wonderfully strange and unsettling way of writing about the forest and nature, and the attempt to wrangle nature. The environment has a will of its own, almost.

These are seeds that were planted for my own novel, and it’s very much the same mindset I had while writing Observer. The landscape is alive and even aware of you in some way that can’t be ascribed to human consciousness. It’s bigger and more diffuse than that.

In In the Woods, there are incredible moments when someone is out by themselves, an almost psychedelic thing happens where they lose themselves or their grip on reality.

I love that novel, and the whole ‘Dublin Murder Squad’ series. They are all very good books, and all very different. Each novel in the series seems to emphasise different elements of the genre. Like, in the next one, one of the detectives discovers a dead body that is her exact doppelganger. She infiltrates a group that this person was in, because they don’t realise that this person is dead.

Perfect, thanks. Let’s talk next about The Woman in White, the Victorian sensation novel by Wilkie Collins.

I think Wilkie Collins is an incredible writer. He was an contemporary of Charles Dickens, but – like Dickens – you will be surprised by how contemporary he sounds. I was really torn between this and his book The Moonstone which is also really incredible, but more of a detective novel.

The Woman in White has been adapted in a game of Telephone – Sarah Waters wrote Fingersmith, which is almost a retelling of The Woman in White, then the South Korean filmmaker Park Chan-Wook adapted Sarah Waters novel as The Handmaiden. I saw The Handmaiden first, then read the novel, then went all the way back to the source material, which is so complex and rich.

Essentially, it’s about the involuntary institutionalisation of women, and the inconvenience of women in certain parts of society and how they have been hidden away. Out of that comes a kind of mystery, in which people are trying to figure out what has happened to other people, and they come up against a very well-funded bureaucracy that is the legal system, and also the social mores of England at the time.

Collins’ writing is deeply suspenseful. There are elements of the Gothic that come through, and – like In the Woods – there are times when it feels like a ghost will appear.

Wilkie Collins has a genuine curiosity and empathy for people in desperate circumstances. Dickens was obviously given a lot of credit for writing about child labour and the social ills of England. They were buddies. Collins is very interesting about the psyche of British aristocrats and those who come into contact with them.

He’s also a very funny writer. You can pick up The Woman in White today and find a very fun page-turner.

Next you’ve chosen to recommend Dorothy B. Hughes’s In A Lonely Place, which was first published in 1947.

This is very much a noir and has a kind of pulpy feel to it. But what elevates it – although I hesitate to call it that, as that suggests the mystery genre is somehow lower – is that we view the novel through the mindset of the antagonist. That is not a spoiler at all, you are very much in his head, seeing his very broken view of the world.

He’s a veteran, adrift in Los Angeles, and he has a very intense misogyny that plays out in an interesting way. He, at once, cannot be alone, but he also hates the company of women. It’s women that he is killing.

So, it’s a novel where you already know who the killer is. So the mystery is in how and whether he is going to be caught. One of his good friends is a police officer, but – without spoiling the novel – it won’t be the police who figure it out. If anything, the police are too preoccupied with their idea of what a criminal should look like that they can’t see what’s in front of them.

It’s a very short novel, but still the right size, because it’s a very visceral experience to be inside this person’s head. To sustain it for longer would be too much, I think. Dorothy B. Hughes’s writing is incredible. I can hear the voice in my head; it’s moody and fully-formed.

They made a film adaptation with Humphrey Bogart. It’s fine, but they changed a lot and to the detriment of the film, frankly. But the novel is really good. You feel… not empathy for the guy, but you do come to understand him. He becomes legible to you in a way that I think is rare in mystery novels, which can be more interested in pathologizing criminality or aberrant behaviour. In this, you come to understand very deeply why he feels that way, although it does not lead you to necessarily want to save him.

What is it about Los Angeles that makes it so suitable for noir?

That’s a good question. So many standout noirs take place in Los Angeles.

I think there’s a duality to L.A., right? It’s so temperate, so idyllic, and then the entertainment industry functions as its crown jewel. I almost included Connie Willis’s Remake, but it didn’t feel quite right. It’s a kind of sci-fi mystery – and, spoiler alert, the next two books on this list are also both sci-fi mystery novels.

Remake takes place in a future Hollywood, in which all the studios are conglomerated, and instead of making new movies they basically generate them with AI. We’re heading there now. All of this really shady stuff is happening in the background, or being allowed to happen while everyone is distracted. I think L.A. is a great proving ground for that kind of narrative; there’s always something you’re not really paying attention to. There are the people in the front, but also the people in the back, right? The people being made to deal with the consequences of the actions of the people you are paying attention to.

I think that’s so much more exaggerated in L.A., and it makes for a very fun setting for bad things to happen.

Brilliant. Can we talk next about A Borrowed Man by Gene Wolfe? It’s a book I was not familiar with at all.

Yes, so Gene Wolfe was a sci-fi fantasy writer from the 1970s right up into the 2010s. He’s one of my favourite writers. He uses a lot of literary references in his prose. He’s often compared to Melville – not because it’s obscure, but because it can be challenging at times, on the level of plot. Sometimes there’s a feeling that you don’t know what’s going on. But his sentences are beautiful.

A Borrowed Man has an interesting premise. It takes place in a future where you can rent out, at the library, cloned reproductions of authors. These clones are downloaded with all the essential memories of these authors. There’s a sequel, Interlibrary Loan, in which a woman is trying to solve a murder by checking out a mystery writer instead of going to the police.

Very good.

It’s very meta. But A Borrowed Man is very fun, very twisty, and very cerebral in places. His references can be quite philosophical. Obviously this clone is wrestling with the idea that he is not technically a person, because he was created, and because his memories are not exactly his.

Gene Wolfe is most well-known for his four-novel series ‘The Book of the New Sun.’ In comparison, this is very different. It has stripped-back language. It’s kind of sparse in places. And both A Borrowed Man and Interlibrary Loan are not very long at all. But worth seeking out. They are really weird.

That’s what I love to hear. I love a mash-up. One of my favourite books is China Mieville’s The City & the City, which is a hardboiled noir set within a very weird, speculative, political situation.

Yes, I just finished his new novel The Rouse, which is, like, 1200 pages long. It’s incredible. I also had the honour of interviewing him a few weeks ago for Defector. The Rouse is a horror novel, but a large part of it is about British counterinsurgency. It’s wild. He does such a great job of mashing things up together and seeing what comes out.

The City & the City is a really great example of a noir that is also sort of metaphysical. Vaguely fantasy. I don’t know exactly what it is, and that is to its credit. That’s what makes it so good.

I should guide us back to your list of recommendations, which concludes with The Dead Mountaineer’s Inn by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky.

Yes, the Strugatsky brothers. They are probably most famous for this novel called Roadside Picnic, which was adapted by Andrei Tarkovsky into his film Stalker. They are Russian satirists who wrote a lot of genre novels. Their stuff was very political and was censored by the Soviet government.

In The Dead Mountaineer’s Inn, they are playing with the genre and breaking its rules. It’s a locked-room mystery with a large cast of characters who become trapped at a ski lodge in winter. Everyone is acting very strange. And this guy, a detective character, is trying to figure out what is going on.

This novel plays with the absurdity of mystery novels. Because there is an inherent ridiculousness to the typical Agatha Christie novel, which is to say: all of these details are clues, and they are supposed to add up to something.

Yes. It’s a kind of literary game.

The book is very convoluted at times. There’s a totally opaque process of meeting all these people, seeing them act suspiciously, then it will be a red herring and you realise you’ve been focusing on all the wrong people.

What’s so fun here is that they play with that expectation that it is all going to make sense at the end. They frustrate that at every turn. What is actually going on is not anything close to what the book initially leads you to believe, and it doesn’t cohere in the way that a mystery novel is supposed to cohere – wrapping it all up in a bow at the end, when you come to understand exactly what was going on the whole time. They don’t lay it out for you. The chaos keeps unfolding and, if anything, accrues momentum.

As we go through the novel, which is not very long, so many things are in disarray, and by the end it’s like: Jesus, how did we even get from A to B? Lest it be lost in my description of this novel, I should also say that it is very funny. It’s so ridiculous and people are acting so strangely.

The main guy is kind of a tool. There’s a kind of latent misogyny baked into mystery novels, especially earlier noir novels, and they play with that expectation. It informs how the detective functions in a revealing way: he has biases and blind spots and an inability to pay attention to or even consider certain characters.

It’s been adapted a few times, although I’ve never seen any of the adaptations. I think it might be impossible – you have to be on such a specific wavelength to get what this novel is doing, and to follow its convictions, which are confusing. But it’s a good one, really fun, and it invites you to read it all over again at the end to see what details you weren’t paying attention to that were there the whole time.

Yes and this neatly brings us back to the discussion we had at the beginning of the two different ways to think about ‘literary mystery novels’: that you can have high-quality examples of the genre, like Tana French’s In the Woods, and then the other kind, which is all about exploding conventions, like The Dead Mountaineer’s Inn.

Also, I was talking to the writer Stephen Graham Jones recently. He’s a horror writer and he was talking about how there’s a very big horror moment going on right now, at least in the States. He speculated that this is because horror, as a genre – as terrifying as it can be – has an ending. At the moment, everything is so horrible already. It feels unending, but horror novels, no matter what, give you an ending.

And that’s true of mystery novels too. In the main.

Although what interests me about most of the novels I was talking about today, and was the project of my novel Observer, is that they have a conclusion but they don’t necessarily leave you with that feeling of catharsis or true resolution. There’s a sense of something not quite finished, or that this is only part of a larger narrative that you don’t get to see. To me, that’s more interesting than the novel that is neatly tied up with a bow.

Five Books aims to keep its book recommendations and interviews up to date. If you are the interviewee and would like to update your choice of books (or even just what you say about them) please email us at [email protected]

Nicholas Russell is a writer from Las Vegas. His work has been featured in McSweeney's, The Guardian, The Baffler, and Film Comment, among other publications. His debut novel Observer is published by Ecco.

entries.title: The Best Nonfiction Books of 2026: The Baillie Gifford Prize Shortlist, recommended by Kirsty Lang
entries.summary: “'Tis strange—but true; for truth is always strange; stranger than fiction,” wrote Lord Byron. For more than a quarter of a century, the Baillie Gifford Prize has celebrated the best nonfiction book of the year. Broadcaster Kirsty Lang, chair of this year's judging panel, talks us through the six books shortlisted for the 2026 prize, from Alexander the Great to Barbara Cartland. This interview app
entries.content:
For those who haven’t come across it, could you introduce the Baillie Gifford Prize and explain what kind of books you’re looking for as judges?

The Baillie Gifford Prize is one of the most important nonfiction book prizes in the English language. It was formerly known as the Samuel Johnson Prize, and has been going since 1999.

What the judges are looking for is good narrative nonfiction. It must be nonfiction with a literary quality, rather than, say, a very academic book. It should have evidence of original research, and a copy-and-paste job will not do.

So it’s got to be original, readable, and have wide appeal. But by wide appeal, I don’t mean dumbing down. We have some very smart books on the list.

The prize rewards quality narrative nonfiction. It should read like a good novel, but be true.

Let’s go through the books that have been shortlisted for the 2026 prize. Can we start with the one that goes furthest back in time? This is Alexander: God, King, and Man by Edmund Richardson. This is a biography of Alexander the Great, but written a bit like fiction. Tell me more.

Everybody who’s rushing to read Homer’s Odyssey after the Christopher Nolan film will love this book. Although Edmund Richardson is a professor of classics at Durham University, he’s written it so it’s very immersive—like a cinematic page-turner. It reminded me of those old-fashioned sword-and-sandal films. You feel that you’re there watching these people.

At the same time, it’s packed with new research. He drew on source material from about a dozen ancient languages. He then uses modern technology to cross-reference and do data analysis. This allows him to go into amazing details like, ‘Given the supply chains, would they have been hungry?’ ‘How hot would it have been? Landscapes have changed –  would they be marching through desert or would it have been savanna?’ You get a real sense of the landscape.

It’s also a fascinating lesson in leadership. Alexander was really young, and he persuaded thousands of men to march into unknown lands across thousands of miles—from ancient Macedon, through ancient Greece, Egypt. He pursued the Persian king, Darius, right across Persia into India.

They didn’t have maps; they didn’t know where they were going—they believed they were going to fall off the existing world. How did Alexander persuade people to follow him? Edward Richardson says he was a great storyteller and had a good story to tell about why they should keep following him and conquering lands. He also doesn’t flinch from Alexander’s brutality.

Yes, I was going to ask: what picture of Alexander emerges from the book?

You spend quite a lot of time wondering what motivates him. In the beginning, he’s broke. He inherits a country where the coffers are empty. Initially, it’s a moneymaking expedition. You conquer and you plunder and everybody gets rich. But there’s a certain point in his travels where he could have said, ‘We’re all rich enough now, we can go home.’ But he doesn’t. He carries on. I came to the conclusion that Alexander was good at battles and less good at ruling because ruling is boring—people moaning about paying taxes or not having water etc. He liked a good battle.

Let’s turn to another book on the 2026 shortlist. What can you tell me about Baldwin: A Love Story by Nicholas Boggs?

This is the first biography of James Baldwin in 30 years. He was a very important figure in the civil rights movement and a very good writer of both fiction and nonfiction. Baldwin is having another moment because he was a very good public speaker. A lot of his speeches and debates with right-wing racists are now emerging again on YouTube, so a new generation is discovering him.

It’s the first biography to look at Baldwin through the prism of his love life. It’s divided into four sections, and each one is about one of the four most important loves of Baldwin’s life. I was a little bit sceptical at first because I thought, ‘Are you therefore reducing him? Are you just focusing on him as a gay man?’ But, actually, what Boggs explains is that a lot of Baldwin’s ideas about race, about masculinity, about gender, were all intertwined. He argued that America’s racial problems were tied up with this myth of white American masculinity—your John Waynes and your Charlton Hestons.

I mention Charlton Heston because one of the stories in the book that I was most surprised by is that at a certain point, Columbia Pictures hired Baldwin to write a script about the life of Malcolm X. They suggested to him that Charlton Heston might be a good candidate to play the role, blacked up.

The book is relevant now, post-Black Lives Matter. A lot of people are disappointed with the rise of white supremacy and racism in the United States, the continuing violence against African American men, and are rediscovering James Baldwin.

Boggs also writes really well. Again, it doesn’t sanctify Baldwin. It shows his blemishes. Like a lot of artists and writers, he was brilliant, but he was also quite selfish and self-obsessed. When it comes to gender, he’s not perfect around feminism by any means. He had strong female friendships and there’s quite a shocking passage where a female friend shares the fact that she has been sexually molested by somebody. The response in his letter almost brushes over it.

But, towards the end of his life, you can see that his views around gender are shifting. He writes a lot about androgyny and how all of us contain some male and some female. He also writes about how we all contain black and white, as we are all descended from Africans.

Then there is Baldwin’s message of love—that the only way you can really combat racism and all forms of prejudice is to learn to love each other. This is a very important message, which I think is very relevant to now.

Nicholas Boggs has spent 20 or so years writing this biography. It’s an extraordinary labour of love: with lots of new original research, letters that hadn’t been seen before, and so on. It’s a super interesting life.

Let’s go on to Days of Love and Rage: A Story of Revolution by Anand Gopal. This is about the Syrian uprising of 2011, although it starts a bit before.

There are so many stories in this book. It’s so moving and tragic and sad, but it’s very readable. Anand Gopal takes us through a very complicated historical event. He starts in the years just before the Arab Spring and takes us through the Syrian civil war by telling the stories of this diverse group of ordinary Syrians living in a town called Manbij.

You get to know the characters—about their childhood, who they fall in love with, who their parents are. Then they come together at a certain point and carry out an experiment in democracy. They’re trying to figure out how to run their town: who is going to collect the rubbish, who is going to police it. They fall out and have arguments and the war carries on. Then ISIS comes into town as well. You experience all this through these characters.

I’m a big fan of the great American reporter Martha Gellhorn, who reported from the Spanish Civil War. She always argued that her form of reporting was a view from the ground, not from the elites or the great men. It was about how ordinary people went through conflict, and this book is a really good example.

In their review, the New York Times compared this book to Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia. You have the euphoria of revolution, and then you have the collapse, the sense of betrayal when it fails.

You really feel for the people, the individual stories. I’m reading this book again now, and thinking about the lack of empathy we have for people escaping from conflict zones. When you read a book like this, you really understand people’s lives in minute detail and what they’ve had to go through and why they might be compelled to flee their country.

On a wider scale, I think the book makes some interesting points about revolution: you see parallels with the French Revolution and the Russian Revolution. It’s this desire for people living under autocracy to rule themselves, to have some say, some control over their lives, but, sadly, this experiment ends in terrible violence.

It’s an extraordinary piece of reporting. Anand Gopal writes for the New Yorker. He heard about this town, Manbij, and went there in 2017 to report on it. By then, they’re very suspicious. They don’t really want to talk to an American of all people. America’s let them down. There are lots of places in the book where they really hope the Americans will come and save them, and of course they never come—despite Obama’s red lines.

So what Gopal does is he recruits some of the participants in the story, and he says, ‘Okay, you record your friends.’ There are something like 2000 interviews and hours and hours of tape, which he weaves together into this extraordinary piece of narrative writing. It’s like a jigsaw puzzle, or some beautifully woven tapestry.

Now we’ve got a book which is set closer to home. This is London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe. He’s another very good writer who has won the Baillie Gifford Prize before for his book about the opioid crisis, Empire of Pain. What’s the story he’s telling in this book?

This is a compelling narrative about the tragic death of a London teenager, Zac Brettler. After his death, his parents found out he had been leading a double life, posing as a Russian oligarch’s son. Possibly he’d been inspired by the wealthy children around him at a very expensive North London private school, or it could have been things he saw online, but he wanted that lifestyle.

A lot of young people are reading this book, and it is quite a publishing phenomenon in terms of the demographics it’s reaching. I asked my 25-year-old goddaughter why she liked it, and she said it’s because she comes from a generation where they’re used to people leading double or alternative lives online. The fact that he wanted that life with a fancy car, pretending that he lived in a really expensive apartment building, is all part of the influencer culture.

As a parent, anybody who’s ever had teenagers will relate to this book. How well do you know your teenager? How much do you know about what they’re doing? Then there is the guilt when you find out you had no idea.

What I also really liked about the book is that Radden Keefe then zooms out and produces a portrait of London, a city which has been completely transformed in the course of my lifetime. Starting with the Big Bang and deregulation of the money markets in the 1980s, huge wealth came into London. Some of it was legitimate, some of it illegitimate. It became a magnet for foreign money. That lifted the city and, in many ways, it is a richer and more attractive city than it was. But it also brought in some pretty unpleasant people.

As well as being this tragic, personal story, the book is almost like a thriller involving Russian money and international crime. It’s also a book about personal secrets. There are quite a lot of secrets being held, not least by Zac’s grandfather, who also had a secret life.

It’s a page-turner, a jolly good read. Patrick Radden Keefe brought his outsider’s eye to the troubles in Northern Ireland with his book Say Nothing, and I think he’s done it again with London in London Falling.

Is it the story of a corrupt London?

Yes. It’s an almost Dickensian portrait of modern London because you’ve got all these extraordinary characters in it. It’s about the dark underbelly of the city, which this kid gets drawn into through his lies.

You also have this interweaving between respectable London society, people who have got wealthy in legitimate ways, and people who haven’t. Unfortunately Zac, by pretending to be a Russian oligarch’s son, was targeted by some criminals who thought he was a rich boy, and then got very angry when they found out he wasn’t.

Okay, we’re now at the fifth book on the shortlist. It’s called The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet. Could you maybe start by telling us who Barbara Cartland was?

Barbara Cartland was probably the most prolific romantic novelist ever. She wrote 723 books, and the reason this biography is called The Great Dictator is that she dictated most of them.

Most people in Britain of a certain age know who Barbara Cartland was because she was a larger-than-life character. She was this extraordinary figure who always dressed in pink, usually pink taffeta. She had these unbelievably long black false eyelashes, which she coated with boot polish because she thought that was more effective than mascara. She was always pictured on a chaise longue, surrounded by small white fluffy Pekinese dogs, and that’s how she dictated her books.

What attracted us to the book was that it’s also a compelling piece of social history. Barbara Cartland lived from 1901 to 2000, so her life maps onto the 20th century. It’s a very British story, and it tells you a lot about the British class system. She was born into a quite upper-class Edwardian family, but they lost their money. You could say that Barbara was driven, for the rest of her life, by wanting to recoup that wealth.

She comes of age in the Roaring Twenties and is one of the bright young things immortalised by Evelyn Waugh. That’s when she’s coming out and trying to find a husband, but the men of her generation have fought in the trenches and are traumatised by the First World War.

She has two younger brothers, who she loses in the Second World War. One of them was a Conservative MP. Barbara Cartland was very anti-Nazi in the 1930s, at a time when a lot of her class were not. That was partly the influence of her younger brother, who was a friend of Churchill, and was arguing at the time of appeasement that we needed to be more wary of Hitler.

The other thing that really impressed us was that it would be really easy for Matthew Sweet, as a writer, to make fun of her, but he doesn’t. It’s funny—don’t get me wrong—because she’s an inherently comical figure in some ways. But he treats her with respect. She’s an outrageous snob, but he doesn’t need to tell you that. He’s showing, not telling, and I think that’s important in nonfiction: I hate to be told what to think about somebody.

He paints this very vivid portrait of her. She was a very paradoxical person. Every single book she wrote followed pretty much the same template: a woman falls in love with a man, and then immediately becomes a good wife and gives up working. Barbara Cartland didn’t really believe that women should work, so whenever she was interviewed and asked about her work, she said, ‘I’m not a working woman. I’m just writing stories.’ But she was the main breadwinner and very active in the war. After the war, she became a local councillor. She was a busy lady, and not one who was happy to sit at home raising the kids. She wanted to get out there, but that contradicted her romantic ideas.

You feel slightly sorry for her oldest daughter, Raine. Most British people will know that Raine married not just one member of the aristocracy, but three—the final husband being Princess Diana’s father. So she was Lady Spencer, immortalised in the papers as ‘Acid Raine’ by her stepchildren. Reading this book, you feel Raine is almost like an experiment for her mother. She tells her off for being too clever at school. She’s always telling Raine she needs to be attractive to men. She’s expected to marry well, and that means money and a title. She’s almost creating one of these characters in the book.

And is Barbara Cartland a dictator in both senses of the word—was she incredibly bossy?

She was incredibly bossy, but I think ‘the great dictator’ refers to the fact that she dictated her books and she was unbelievably prolific. She had 723 books published, and then Matthew Sweet is given access to her house and finds she’s written about another 100 unpublished books.

It’s impressive, even if the plots and characters are formulaic.

They sold in the millions. Women bought these books. They provided escapism. I’ve got a South African brother-in-law who grew up in a township where there were very few books. His mother was a cleaner, and she used to bring back books from other people’s houses, so he read Barbara Cartland when he was young in South Africa.

Finally, we have another biography: The Traveller: The Revolutionary Life of George Forster and his Search for Humanity by Andrea Wulf.

I love this book. It’s about a forgotten figure from history, George Forster (1754-1794). He was an explorer and an anthropologist. As a 17-year-old, he went on Captain Cook’s second voyage, and Wulf explains in the book that she actually goes to these places—the southern tip of New Zealand, the South Pacific. She travels in Forster’s footsteps, and it’s this really vivid, immersive piece of writing.

Then there is her research. Wulf has access to the German archives—his letters and his diaries. Forster was himself a very good writer. In fact, he wrote up the Captain Cook voyage, and it was a bestselling travel book in the 18th century.  He was quite famous, travelling round Europe, and being invited to courts to tell his stories.

What made him quite special was that, unlike most Europeans at that time, he did not see the indigenous peoples that he encountered on the Cook voyage as inferior in any way. He saw them as equals. At that time, most Europeans assumed that they were superior and were bringing civilization to these places, but he was a humanist. He saw them as members of society that had evolved differently from Europeans, and made a real effort to learn their languages and their customs.

He went on to have a really interesting life. He became an academic in various European universities. He was also a feminist. He married a woman who treated him appallingly. They had an open marriage and she had all these affairs. He didn’t have affairs, but felt she needed the freedom to express herself.

He also has this awful father who is a botanist and takes him across Catherine the Great’s Russia as a child. I think that’s where the empathy comes from. If, at age ten, you’re dragged across Russia for several years, then you go to London in your teens and have to learn English—and are completely self-taught—then, at age 17, you go on Captain Cook’s voyage, you learn to see different perspectives. At a time when most people grow up in their village and never leave it, his knowledge of the world was extraordinary at a very young age.

Finally, at the end of the century, he becomes a revolutionary and moves to Paris. He takes part in the French Revolution, which, inevitably, he sees descend into terror, and he dies a very disappointed man.

So it’s an incredible life. She’s a beautiful writer.

It sounds like an extraordinary window into the 18th century.

Absolutely. It’s a story of the Enlightenment as well. Wulf has written a lot about the 18th century—she has a book about Alexander von Humboldt, The Invention of Nature. Her last book, Magnificent Rebels, was about the German Romantics. It was a really interesting period.

Thank you so much for introducing these books. It’s a great range of books on the shortlist this year. Was it hard getting it down to just six?

This year was a very strong year for non-fiction, so it was very tough coming up with the shortlist. I’m proud of it because it is very varied. To have a list that includes Barbara Cartland and the Syrian Revolution, as well as Alexander the Great, is quite an achievement.

They’re very rich books. I’ve really enjoyed reading all of them.
